results.subject: Cornershop — Brimful of Asha
results.headline: The Remix That Reframed “Brimful of Asha”
results.article:
Cornershop’s “Brimful of Asha” began its chart life in 1997 as a Wiiija release from When I Was Born for the 7th Time, the English alternative rock band’s third album. In its original form, the single reached number 60 on the UK Singles Chart.

The record’s second run followed a remix by Norman Cook, working as Fatboy Slim. That version became a radio and critical success, changing the scale of the song’s release without changing its identity as a Cornershop recording. Re-released in the UK, “Brimful of Asha” rose from its earlier number 60 placing to number one.

Its reach extended beyond the UK chart: the remixed release also reached number 16 on the US Billboard Modern Rock Tracks chart. The two chart results mark two sharply different public moments for the same 1997 song—first as an original Wiiija single, then as a re-released record reshaped by Cook’s remix.

results.subject: Men Without Hats — The Safety Dance
results.headline: ‘The Safety Dance’ and the Productive Oddness of a Pop Title
results.article:
Released in 1983, Men Without Hats’ “The Safety Dance” begins, at least on the page, with a phrase that refuses to settle into ordinary pop-language logic. “Safety” suggests caution, procedure and restraint; “dance” suggests motion, bodies and the possibility of disorder. Putting the two together creates a miniature contradiction before a listener has even pressed play.

That contradiction is the title’s durable trick. It is simple enough to say aloud, yet strange enough to invite a second look. Rather than offering a standard declaration of romance, nightlife or rebellion, the wording sounds like a rule that may not be a rule at all. Its appeal lies in that unresolved tone: is it protective, ironic, earnest, or simply absurd?

Men Without Hats’ title also has the compact shape of a chant. Four small words can function as a slogan, a command, or a question depending on the delivery imagined by the listener. The available context includes a performance video, a fitting extension of a title already built around action. In 1983, “The Safety Dance” gave Men Without Hats a nameable, repeatable paradox: movement framed by caution, with neither side fully winning.
